articles.title: Madras High Court pulls up T.N. HR&CE department for failing to act promptly against an erring EO in 2011
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Madras High Court has deprecated the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) department for not having taken prompt action in 2011 against an Executive Officer (EO) for permitting tenants to put up permanent constructions on temple lands and not taking steps to cancel the patta (revenue document on land ownership) obtained by private individuals for temple properties.

The Second Division Bench of Justices S.M. Subramaniam and Krishnaswamy Govindarajan said that the charges levelled against R. Jayakumar, when he served as the EO of Thiyagaraja Swamy Temple in Tiruvarur in 2011, presented “a classic case of the fence eating the crops” since he had colluded with the tenants and allowed them to usurp valuable temple lands, which he was duty-bound to protect.

Pointing out that the former EO was also accused of unauthorisedly releasing ₹40 lakh of temple funds to a civil contractor, the judges said that “unfortunately, the HR&CE Commissioner at that time did not take the issue seriously,” and sat over the matter despite complaints made by devotees and others. To add salt to the wound, the Commissioner called for a report from the officer against whom allegations had been levelled.

“Sitting on the issue for a prolonged period and allowing illegalities to continue is highly deprecated. The sequence of events proves poor management by the department, with no checks and balances. Only because of complaints by devotees and the Adheenam did the mismanagement come to light, leading to the initiation of action and the dismissal of the EO from service in 2015,” the Bench said.

Authoring the verdict, Justice Govindarajan said that a single judge of the High Court ought not to have interfered with the punishment imposed on the individual and ordered that it should be modified to the denial of promotion for a period of five years. The Bench allowed a State appeal and set aside the single judge’s 2024 order directing the HR&CE department to reinstate the writ petitioner in service.

“Modifying a punishment under Article 226 (writ jurisdiction) of the Constitution is legally unsustainable and contrary to service jurisprudence. Having found that mismanagement was committed by the writ petitioner, the only choice available to the authorities was removal from service. In our view, the punishment of dismissal is not disproportionate, and all legal formalities were duly followed prior to issuing the dismissal order,” the Bench concluded.

articles.title: Tourists visiting Valparai cautioned to keep safe distance from wild animals moving along roads
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Forest Department has advised tourists visiting Valparai to be cautious while driving past wild animals and not to approach them to click photos after a video of two gaurs charging at motorists at Cinchona went viral.
According to Forest Department officials, the gaurs seen in the video were into a rutting battle, a typical behaviour in males to establish dominance and mating rights.

Two male gaurs that were into a rutting battle charged at motorists at Cinchona near #Valparai on Wednesday, October 21. The motorists were unaware of the sparring going on between the two bulls. Forest Department officials said no one was injured in the incident. @THChennai https://t.co/AuiMdxfurE

“A sparring was going on between the two gaurs and the tourists were not aware of it. It is normal for gaurs to take brief breaks during the rutting battle. As the two gaurs were standing on either sides of the road, the tourists must have believed that they were grazing. The gaurs felt disturbed when the tourists passed through the road and charged at them,” said K. Giritharan, Forest Range Officer, Manambolly range.
He said that the Forest Department staff later spoke to the tourists and none of them suffered injuries in the incident. However, their two-wheelers had a few damages.

Gaurs are found in large numbers in the Valparai plateau, which falls within the jurisdictions of the Anamalai Tiger Reserve. They are also found in tea and coffee estates, which are interspersed with forest areas. While local residents are aware of their movement and behaviour, tourists often stop vehicles upon spotting gaurs and other wild animals out of curiosity.
Mr. Giritharan said that tourists must avoid approaching wild animals or disturbing them by taking photographs or videos. Similarly, feeding of wild animals should also be avoided.
“Tourists are advised to halt vehicles at a distance when wild animals like gaurs or elephants are on the roads. Resume the journey after the animals move away,” he added.

articles.title: Use of Tamil Nadu CM Vijay’s deep fake videos to collect money: Rajasthan youth moves Madras High Court seeking bail
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A Rajasthan youth arrested by Tamil Nadu police, for reportedly using deep fake videos of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay to collect money from gullible people, has approached the Madras High Court seeking bail in the case booked by the Cyber Crime Cell of Crime Branch-Criminal Investigation Department (CB-CID).

The plea has been listed for hearing before Justice N. Ramesh on Friday (October 23, 2026). Petitioner J. Shyabu Khan, 28, of Boontoli village in Alwar district of Rajasthan was arrested on September 12, 2026 and brought to Tamil Nadu on a transit warrant before being lodged at a local prison here pursuant to his remand.

The charge against him was that he created Facebook accounts titled ‘All India help Vijay Thalapati’ and ‘All India help’ in which the AI-generated deep fake videos of the Chief Minister were used promising help to people in need if they get themselves registered on payment of registration fees to a particular UPI number.

The cybercrime cell had come across the deep fake videos during regular cyber patrolling, tracked down the IP addresses to Boontoli and nabbed the petitioner with the assistance of Rajasthan police. The Principal Sessions Court in Chennai had on October 14, 2026 refused to gant bail to the petitioner.

Though the petitioner claimed his friend Sakrulla had created the impersonating videos, used his Facebook ID, mobile phone number as well as bank account to commit the crime, the sessions court refused to grant bail since the investigation was yet to be completed.

In his present bail plea before the High Court too, the petitioner claimed to be innocent and said his family had been put to great prejudice because of his incarceration for the last 40 days. He agreed to abide by any condition imposed by the court for the purpose of grant of bail.

The petitioner also claimed the police had arrested him without ascertaining the true facts and said the investigation must have got almost over by now as more than a month had lapsed since his arrest.

articles.title: All 14 Indians in yacht incident off Yemen coast reported safe: Embassy
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: India on Friday (October 23, 2026) said that its 14 nationals onboard a yacht involved in an incident off the coast of Yemen are safe and it will continue to work to ensure their well-being.

Some Arab media on Thursday (October 22, 2026) quoted Yemen’s Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree as claiming that Saudi forces targeted the Indian yacht near Yuqar Island near the Yemeni coast in the Red Sea.
Saree said that the yacht is carrying 14 Indian nationals and that Houthi forces are rescuing them. He said more details would be provided later.
“Reports suggest that all 14 Indian nationals are safe and located around Hodeidah in Yemen,” the Indian mission posted on social media on Friday (October 23, 2026).
“We will continue to work for ensuring their well-being,” it said.
The Indian embassy has not yet specifically commented on the source of the attack on the yacht.
Earlier, the Indian embassy said it has reached out to different parties to “establish circumstances and facts” surrounding the incident.
The incident comes amid an escalation of hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with both sides targeting each other’s facilities and infrastructure.

The Indian Embassy on Thursday (October 23, 2026) also said it was ascertaining details about an incident involving 14 Indian nationals on board a yacht off the coast of Yemen and would provide all possible help to ensure their safety, amid escalating tensions in the region.
An Indian national was killed and three others injured in two separate attacks on a major airport and an oil field in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday (October 21, 2026).

articles.title: TVK, DMK walk out of Chief Electoral Officer’s meeting on Special Summary Revision in Tamil Nadu
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Nine of the 12 recognised national and State political parties that attended a meeting convened by Chief Electoral Officer Archana Patnaik at the Secretariat in Chennai on Friday (October 23, 2026) to discuss the upcoming Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls walked out after recording their views and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The ruling TVK and its allies, as well as the DMK, the principal Opposition party, were among those that staged the walkout. The Election Commission of India (ECI) had invited six recognised national parties such as the Congress, the BJP, the BSP, the AAP, the CPI(M), and the NPP, as well as seven recognised State parties such as the TVK, the DMK, the AIADMK, the CPI, the NTK, the VCK, and the DMDK, to take part in the meeting to discuss the SSR.

Barring the BSP, the other 12 parties participated in the meeting. Representatives of the BJP, the AIADMK, and the NPP were among those who did not stage a walkout, while others walked out at various stages of the meeting, with some recording their views before leaving.

Minister for Energy Resources and Law C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar, who attended the meeting on behalf of the TVK, told reporters after the walkout that the SSR was unnecessary when the errors in the SIR had not yet been rectified. He alleged that a large number of voters had been deleted from the electoral rolls during the SIR. He said his party had passed resolutions and held protests against the SIR even before the elections. He also demanded the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner.

Former DMK MLA I. Paranthaman said the party had conveyed its views, highlighting the concerns of the people, before staging a walkout. He said the SIR exercise had been marked by several irregularities, which the DMK had repeatedly flagged even before the elections. As many as 74 lakh voters had been deleted from the electoral rolls, he said, questioning what steps the ECI had taken to enrol eligible voters.

“The ECI should be people-friendly and facilitate the enrolment of eligible voters. While campaigning for 100% voter turnout, the Commission was, on the other hand, creating obstacles to the inclusion of eligible electors in the electoral rolls,” he alleged.
He said a resolution demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner had already been adopted at a meeting of DMK MPs.

Former VCK MLA S.S. Balaji said the SIR exercise had been justified on the grounds of removing infiltrators from the electoral rolls. However, the ECI had not provided any clarity to the public on how many such persons had been identified, the methods used to identify them or the action taken against them. “Instead, the ECI was proceeding with the subsequent SSR after the SIR as though nothing had happened during the earlier exercise,” he alleged.

articles.title: India-Poland strategic partnership should translate into JVs: PM Donald Tusk
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: “India and Poland should move beyond traditional trade and deepen cooperation in technology, AI and aerospace to strengthen their economies”, Poland Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday (October 23, 2026).

Strategic partnership between the two countries should translate into Joint Ventures (JVs), the visiting leader said, addressing the India-Poland Business Forum at Bengaluru. He called for greater technological cooperation between the two countries to strengthen their economies and help them access global markets.
Mr. Tusk highlighted the city's role as a global technology and innovation hub.
"This place (Bengaluru) shows how investing in people, knowledge, and entrepreneurship can change the position of the entire economy," he added.

Recalling that India and Poland elevated their ties to a strategic partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Warsaw in August 2024, Mr. Tusk said the action plan covered technological cooperation, cybersecurity and the space sector.
Mr. Tusk added that cooperation between the two countries should strengthen both economies and help them compete in global markets.

On information technology and digitisation, the Polish leader proposed partnerships combining India's large IT services sector with his country's expertise in software, cloud solutions, automation and cybersecurity. He said Polish companies could bring specialised solutions and European market experience, while Indian partners could help scale production and services.

Highlighting digital public services, he cited India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and Poland's electronic government services and mObywatel digital identity application as examples of expertise the countries could share.

"Together we can develop secure solutions that make everyday life easier for citizens and businesses," he said, stressing that digitalisation should improve productivity, reduce costs and enhance service quality.

Mr. Tusk said Artificial Intelligence (AI) should occupy a special place in bilateral cooperation, with opportunities to develop applications for industrial automation, data analysis, diagnostics and infrastructure management.
He also called for tools for small and medium-sized enterprises and greater cooperation between universities and research institutes in machine learning and data analysis.
"Cybersecurity, information protection, and digital infrastructure resilience are therefore both a common challenge and an area of new business opportunities," he said.

articles.title: Economics beyond the individual
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford’s work modelling the macroeconomy based on individual agents’ decisions has significant implications for monetary policy. Despite being hailed as providing a rigorous foundation for stabilisation policies, focusing on the individual blinds us to the way the macroeconomy actually works. It may seem paradoxical; John Maynard Keynes’s insight was that the aggregate economy cannot be understood simply as the sum of individual actions. Heterodox economics, by focusing on the structure of the broader economy rather than its individual components, provides a much better framework for understanding the economy.
The work of Keynes in the wake of the Great Depression led to the development of the study of the aggregate economy, as opposed to studying demand and supply of individual commodities.
Microeconomics focuses on the optimising behaviour of the individual, while macroeconomics focuses on statistical relationships to characterise aggregate behaviour.

Hall and Woodford provided rigorous models that rooted the study of macroeconomic aggregates, such as consumption, investment and employment, in the behaviour of individual agents. A key contribution was linking consumption to interest rates and the future. Individuals chose to smooth consumption over their lifetimes rather than base it solely on their current needs.

When interest rates were high, savings yielded greater returns. Individuals therefore had an incentive to defer some consumption to earn more and consume more in the future. Higher interest rates could reduce current consumption and hence lower current demand, and vice versa. Macroeconomic dynamics could consequently be derived from rigorous formulations of how individuals responded to market signals and policy variables such as interest rates.

This provided a framework within which Central Bankers could target an interest rate that was ‘neutral’ to the real economy — one that neither excessively stimulated nor depressed aggregate demand — greatly aiding the development of sophisticated stabilisation paradigms for monetary policy.

However, this approach collapsed the distinction between consumption, savings and investment. By viewing consumption inter-temporally, and by making it the main component of demand, the microfoundations methodology relegated the importance of volatile investment expectations to the background. Whatever was not consumed currently was saved, and automatically translated into future consumption demand. This was the framework followed by classical economics, which Keynes contested. He cautioned that not all saving is necessarily undertaken for future consumption.

In contrast, investment is fuelled by expectations of business owners as to prospects of profit. There is no necessity for the savings behaviour of individuals to always imply a demand for future consumption, and hence investment, by businesses. How can businesses determine whether an act of individual savings is to spend on a house for the future, or to ward against a future health emergency that may or may not occur? In such a situation, the interest rate cannot serve as an indicator of the extent of future consumption.
Keynes further suggested a radical intervention. It was not the interest rate that equated savings and investment, but income. Investment raised income, and generated an equal amount of savings.

This is not merely a technical insight, but an important way in which to view policy. It is not savings or inter-temporal consumption demand that affects output growth and employment, but business investment. To understand why economies are prone to instability, one must examine the investment behaviour of companies rather than the consumption demands of individuals.

According to Keynes, investment being done for profit in an environment of uncertainty is the chief source of economic instability. In uncertain situations, it is rational for investors to follow the herd, investing during a boom for fear of missing out on speculative returns, and withdrawing investment in a recession for fear of loss. This is the reason why booms and recessions get amplified. The work of Keynesians such as Hyman Minsky and Jan Kregel offers great insight into how the financial behaviour of firms brought about the boom in housing construction and finance, as well as the recession in 2008. Much of the current stock market gains in the U.S. economy are being driven by AI hyperscalers, giving rise to concerns of a new bubble that might eventually burst. Such outcomes can be clearly discerned when viewed from a Keynesian lens.

Some might argue that it does not matter how one views the economy, if the framework designed to bring about stability is effective. Moreover, in centering the actions of individuals, so the argument goes, this framework takes into account the reality of a complex economy being driven by individual choices.

Despite being hailed as providing a rigorous foundation for stabilisation policies, focusing on the individual blinds us to the way the macroeconomy actually works. It may seem paradoxical; John Maynard Keynes’s insight was that the aggregate economy cannot be understood simply as the sum of individual actions. Heterodox economics, by focusing on the structure of the broader economy rather than its individual components, provides a much better framework for understanding the economy.
• The work of Keynes in the wake of the Great Depression led to the development of the study of the aggregate economy, as opposed to studying demand and supply of individual commodities.
• Microeconomics focuses on the optimising behaviour of the individual, while macroeconomics focuses on statistical relationships to characterise aggregate behaviour.

articles.title: Why managing fiscal is a tightrope for State governments
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are among the most socially and economically advanced States in India. Yet, the finances of both governments, like those of most other States, are under stress. The White Papers recently released by the two governments described their outstanding debt as alarming. State government debt is often vilified as the result of fiscal mismanagement. But it may, in fact, reflect a mismatch between development aspirations and the limited fiscal capacity of State governments.

Debts build up over the years with deficits, which arise when the government’s expenditure overshoots its tax and other receipts. In India, while the power to raise taxes rests largely with the Union government, a larger share of overall government spending is borne by the State governments. A majority of the State government expenditure is on social sectors, such as health and education, and economic sectors, such as agriculture and irrigation, all of which have a direct impact on people’s lives and livelihoods. In Kerala, the high levels of State government spending on social sectors since the 1960s have been a central constituent of the public action driving social progress. Compared with the corresponding average for all Indian States, per capita State government social expenditure was higher in Kerala and Tamil Nadu (by 30% and 20%, respectively). In contrast, it was markedly lower in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (by 35% and 40%) (for the period 2020-23, according to an analysis based on State Finances: A Study of Budgets, Reserve Bank of India).

articles.title: The reality behind falling net FDI
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: I ndia’s net foreign direct investment (FDI) has declined drastically in recent years. Critics see the weak net flows as a sign of weakness, while the Chief Economic Adviser points to the large inflows and rising manufacturing FDI as evidence of strength. He links weak net flows to profit repatriation and outward investment by Indian companies.

However, this debate overlooks a major issue. By focusing on overall numbers, both sides ignore the changing composition of international capital and the Balance of Payments (BoP) mechanisms that govern inflows and outflows.

For BoP purposes, net FDI is calculated as the difference between inflows and outflows after adjusting for the repatriation of capital. From the peak of $44.0 billion in 2020-21, net FDI fell to less than $1 billion in 2024-25. It recovered to $7.6 billion in 2025-26. The corresponding gross inflow was $94.6 billion.

It is necessary to note that India’s liberal FDI policy, introduced in 1991, initially emphasised technology acquisition, export promotion, and foreign exchange conservation. Over time, policy increasingly prioritised attracting larger inflows, while concerns regarding future external payment obligations and investment quality receded.

FDI is often viewed as a uniform, long-term commitment that brings technology and management skills to the host country. FDI can fall into three different investor classes, each with distinct capabilities, strategies, and exit timelines.

The first category is real FDI (RFDI), consisting of traditional multinational enterprises with the technology, brands, and capabilities to establish production and services. These generally represent long-term commitments.

The second category comprises financial investors, including private equity funds, venture capital firms, sovereign wealth funds, and asset managers. Their main goal is capital growth and planned exits.

The third category includes diaspora investments and special purpose vehicles (SPVs). These involve capital raised abroad and funneled through offshore financial centres, sometimes including the round-tripping of Indian funds.

Data on remittance-level FDI from the past four years, from 2022-23 to 2025-26 up to December, show that RFDI made up 41.9% of “effective inflows.” Financial investors followed closely with a 40.5% share, while the remaining 17.6% came from the diaspora and SPVs linked to India.

The business model of financial investors suggests future exits that result in large-scale capital repatriations. A notable example occurred in 2025 when Singapore’s Temasek exited Schneider Electric India Ltd., earning $6.4 billion on an investment of $637 million made in 2020. Total recorded divestment in CY 2025 was $52 billion, with 45 major foreign private equity and venture capital exits accounting for $29 billion in outflows.

Based on an analysis of effective inflows, FDI in India’s manufacturing sector has declined across three consecutive four-year periods. Most notably, RFDI into manufacturing accounted for only 10.6% of total effective inflows during the most recent four-year period.

A major blind spot in gross FDI figures is the mixing of new capital injections with corporate accounting changes, such as intra-group ownership reorganisations, mergers, share swaps, and the conversion of earlier non-equity instruments such as external commercial borrowings (ECBs) and convertible debentures.

articles.title: SBI’s cyber defences: What the bank had in place
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The suspected customer-data exposure at State Bank of India (SBI) has brought its cybersecurity preparedness into focus, despite the bank reporting an extensive array of safeguards in its annual disclosures.

SBI’s FY2025–26 Sustainability Report and Annual Report, published before the reported exposure, detail its security audits, automated threat monitoring, incident-response procedures and employee training. The disclosures also outline plans to further integrate its cyber-defence operations.

SBI’s Sustainability Report says information-systems audits covered 427 IT systems during FY26. Audits of outsourced IT activities covered 695 activities, while internal and external cybersecurity audits covered 176 IT applications and infrastructure and 151 systems, respectively.
However, the report does not disclose the findings, the number of vulnerabilities identified or how many were rectified. SBI reported “nil” instances of data breaches during FY26.

The bank’s Global Cyber Security Operations Centre (GCSOC) continuously monitors critical information systems for threats and unauthorised access. Automated tracking of indicators of compromise (IoCs)—digital clues that may signal cyberattacks—has replaced a previously manual process.
SBI also monitors phishing, fraudulent websites, brand impersonation, vishing and rogue mobile applications, pursuing the removal of malicious links and websites.

Its Annual Report cites an automated Secure Configuration Monitoring System covering more than 85,000 IT assets. AI-driven intelligence platforms, risk profiling and continuous monitoring of digital transactions help identify suspicious activity.

Security testing includes ethical hacking, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and red-team exercises across websites, mobile applications, databases, networks and internal systems. Monthly domain-password-spray tests seek to identify employees using easily guessed passwords.
Firewalls, encryption, multi-factor authentication and data-loss prevention tools provide additional safeguards.

CERT SBI serves as the central first responder to cyber incidents. Its response framework covers detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident reviews. A separate Incident Response Wing handles forensic investigations, threat hunting, mock drills and regulatory reporting.

SBI conducted 2,079 information-security and cybersecurity training programmes, benefiting 39,961 employees in FY26. Nearly 1.81 lakh employees had completed mandatory cybersecurity e-learning and assessments by March 31, 2026.
Oversight rests with the Board-level IT Strategy Committee, while the Group Chief Information Security Officer heads the Information Security Department.

fullParagraphs: India on Friday (October 23, 2026) said that its 14 nationals onboard a yacht involved in an incident off the coast of Yemen are safe and it will continue to work to ensure their well-being.

Some Arab media on Thursday (October 22, 2026) quoted Yemen’s Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree as claiming that Saudi forces targeted the Indian yacht near Yuqar Island near the Yemeni coast in the Red Sea.

The Indian embassy has not yet specifically commented on the source of the attack on the yacht.
Earlier, the Indian embassy said it has reached out to different parties to “establish circumstances and facts” surrounding the incident.
The incident comes amid an escalation of hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with both sides targeting each other’s facilities and infrastructure.

The Indian Embassy on Thursday (October 23, 2026) also said it was ascertaining details about an incident involving 14 Indian nationals on board a yacht off the coast of Yemen and would provide all possible help to ensure their safety, amid escalating tensions in the region.

articles.title: What is the importance of the UN Loss and Damage Fund’s payout to Nepal? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Story so far: The United Nations’ climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has approved a $21.6 million pay out (approx. ₹205 crore) to the Nepal government to help with rebuilding , following the devastating floods in August.

Formally, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), was set up to help developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change respond to economic and non-economic losses, including from extreme weather and slow-onset events. It operates under the financial mechanism of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022 , and its Governing Instrument was adopted at COP28 in 2023.

As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions. Its start-up allocation is $342 million with at least half of it reserved for small island developing States and least developed countries. Its first call for funding requests drew 176 requests from 119 countries worth about $2.8 billion (₹26,600 crore). In July the Board deferred decisions on those requests to December.

It is the first time the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country. The Board took the decision at its first “extraordinary meeting,” held virtually on October 22, 2026. It also agreed to pilot, during the start-up phase, an approach allowing Nepal to submit a request outside the closed submission window. Any further such submissions will need separate Board decisions, and the Secretariat will assess lessons for the Fund’s long-term model.

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche, that experts say is linked to climate changed from human-accelerated global warming, set off flooding along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. Nepal estimates economic losses of at least $2.69 billion and recovery needs of at least $4.71 billion. The decision comes weeks before COP31 opens in Turkiye.

The $21.6 million approved by the Board includes $1.6 million in oversight fees, which are paid to the organisations that implement projects to cover the cost of supervising how money is used. Nepal has been invited to submit a funding request, which the Board will consider at its tenth meeting in Manila in December. Money would be released only after that approval.
The Fund has not publicly said how much cash it holds beyond signed contributions, and disbursement depends on donors honouring pledges.

Since its creation at COP27, the Fund has had to show that pledges translate into money for affected countries. The United States, the largest historical emitter, had pledged $17.5 million under President Joe Biden. In January 2025, the Trump administration withdrew the US representatives from the Fund’s board which was part of the US’ larger exit out of the Paris Agreement. At the time, pledges stood at about $741 million.

Jawad Khalid, a climate finance specialist writing for the Lowy Institute, an independent Australian think tank, argued that the Fund “still operates like a conventional development fund” rather than an emergency mechanism. “Its single funding cycle runs eleven steps, from origination through technical review to board approval. The Fund is hosted by the World Bank, which serves as its interim trustee,” he wrote in a piece.

Ajay Mathur, a former Director General of the International Solar Alliance, called the step “landmark” in a media statement. He cautioned that the sum is less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction cost. He noted that cash would flow only after further project proposals are cleared, risking delays to relief.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said in a media statement that while the Fund “took a historic first step” it it “cannot be a one-off.” He said no country should have to wait seven weeks, through “historic letters and relentless pressure,” to unlock an emergency meeting, and called for a permanent rapid-response system that moves support “in days, not months.” He said developed countries insisted the decision must not set a precedent or prejudge the long-term model, adding: “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions.”

Others read the decision more positively. Raju Pandit Chhetri, the Least Developed Countries’ lead climate finance negotiator, said it showed countries could reach “swift, effective consensus” and set “a strong precedent.”

articles.title: Poland’s abortion law: What will the new bills change? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The story so far: Hundreds of women gathered outside Polish Parliament (Sejm) in Warsaw on Thursday (October 22, 2026), braving heavy rain to demand access to free and legal abortion, as demonstrations spread across more than 20 cities in Poland. Signalling rejection of the government’s record, protesters raised pro-choice slogans in a show of anger at Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s failure to deliver on his promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws.

The demonstrations came just two days after the lower house, the Sejm, passed two bills seeking to ease the country’s restrictive abortion laws. The proposed changes seek to roll back some of the restrictions on the rights of abortion imposed under the previous government, but their passage into law remains uncertain, with President Karol Nawrocki expected to veto the measures.

Poland has some of the most restrictive abortion laws in Europe. Since 1993, abortions has been allowed in Catholic Poland only on specific grounds. The restrictions tightened in October 2020, when the country’s Constitutional Tribunal ruled that abortion on the grounds of severe foetal abnormalities was unconstitutional. The ruling came into force in January 2021, effectively establishing a near-total ban on abortion. Since then, and under the current law, legal abortion is when a pregnancy threatens the woman’s life or health, or when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, like rape or incest. In cases involving rape or incest, termination is permitted up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Abortion on request is not permitted in Poland, and women seeking such terminations outside the legal grounds face major barriers to accessing healthcare. The law also criminalises assistance in pursuing an unlawful abortion, with penalties of up to three years’ imprisonment. However, the woman undergoing the abortion is not criminally liable. The restrictions have prompted repeated nationwide protests, including demonstrations in 2016 and after the 2020 ruling, with activists accusing the authorities of curtailing reproductive rights and restricting access to abortion care.

When Mr. Tusk’s coalition, comprising parties ranging from the left to the centre-right, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to liberalise abortion laws. However, disagreements between the coalition’s more conservative and liberal factions stalled reform efforts, fuelling criticism that the government had failed to honour its electoral commitments.
The issue has now returned to the parliamentary agenda, a year ahead of the next parliamentary election. On October 20, the Sejm passed two bills seeking to ease abortion restrictions.

The first bill seeks to partially decriminalise abortion by removing criminal penlties for terminating a pregnancy with a woman’s consent outside the grounds currently permitted by law, as well as for helping or encouraging such an abortion. It also proposes protections from criminal liability for doctors, nurses and midwives who terminate a pregnancy to avert a threat to the woman’s life or health, or in circumstances involving a high probability of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities or an incurable condition threatening the foetus’s life.

The second bill seeks to restore abortion as a legal option when doctors identify a severe and irreversible foetal abnormality or an incurable condition threatening foetal viability. This would reverse the effect of the 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling, which removed foetal abnormalities as a legal ground for termination.

Both bills would need to clear further legislative and presidential hurdles before becoming law. Even if enacted, they would not legalise abortion on request and would leave Catholic Poland’s near-total ban unchanged. Protesters have dismissed the new measures, calling it token gestures rather than a genuine effort to reform the law, arguing that the government is seeking to demonstrate progress on an issue that could influence its prospects in 2027 parliamentary elections.

Abortion laws vary widely across European Union, with countries setting different gestational limits and conditions for access. While several countries permit abortion on request during the first trimester, others maintain restrictive legal frameworks.

France became the first country in the world to explicitly enshrine the freedom to have an abortion in its Constitution in 2024. Abortion is permitted on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy and is covered by the public healthcare system. In Sweden, abortion is permitted on request up to 18 weeks, with medical abortions available at home under approved arrangements and costs covered by the state healthcare system. The Netherlands permits abortion until the foetus is considered capable of surviving outside the womb, generally around 24 weeks in practice, subject to legal and medical requirements.

Spain permits abortion on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy, while Ireland allows it up to 12 weeks. Finland also permits abortion on request during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, following a reform that took effect in 2023. Portugal permits abortion on request up to 10 weeks.

Signalling rejection of the government’s record, protesters raised pro-choice slogans in a show of anger at Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s failure to deliver on his promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws.
• The demonstrations came just two days after the lower house, the Sejm, passed two bills seeking to ease the country’s restrictive abortion laws. The proposed changes seek to roll back some of the restrictions on the rights of abortion imposed under the previous government, but their passage into law remains uncertain, with President Karol Nawrocki expected to veto the measures.
• Poland has some of the most restrictive abortion laws in Europe. Since 1993, abortions has been allowed in Catholic Poland only on specific grounds. The restrictions tightened in October 2020, when the country’s Constitutional Tribunal ruled that abortion on the grounds of severe foetal abnormalities was unconstitutional. The ruling came into force in January 2021, effectively establishing a near-total ban on abortion. Since then, and under the current law, legal abortion is when a pregnancy threatens the woman’s life or health, or when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, like rape or incest. In cases involving rape or incest, termination is permitted up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

articles.title: Airbnb sets down rules to stop hosts from forcing guests to clean homes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Airbnb, a company that facilitates travel accommodation agreements between private property owners and visitors, introduced a new rule that restrains hosts from making their guests perform too many household chores before they leave.

Airbnb hosts, as they are called, are allowed to set certain rules and requirements for the upkeep of their homes and apartments. For example, they could require guests to strip the bedsheets after their visit, take their trash to designated areas, do laundry, sweep floors, or run a dishwashing cycle.
Airbnb guests and hosts rate and review each other based on their experience, which can affect their standing when hosting future guests or visiting other Airbnb properties.
However, Airbnb guests have for years complained that, on top of being forced to carry out onerous household chores while on vacation, many Airbnb property hosts charge extravagant cleaning fees.
Airbnb has recently settled the debate, by stating in plain language that hosts must be “reasonable” and not use their guests as cleaners.

“For example, hosts are generally not allowed to: Ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes,” stated one of the rules in Airbnb’s help centre webpage.
The update has sparked a social media frenzy. Many guests reacted with relief, recounting anecdotes of being forced to do laundry and wash dishes while on holiday—on top of paying a cleaning fee.

Meanwhile, many Airbnb hosts lashed out against the updated rule, pointing out that Airbnb guests could stay at hotels or agree to higher fees if they did not want to do a few light cleaning tasks after their stay. For their part, a number of guests argued that Airbnb prices were almost on par with hotel booking fees—and also required the guest to work while on holiday.
Several hosts found the new rule confusing and felt that more flexibility was required.

“My main issue is it’s letting me ask people to load the dishwasher but I can’t ask them to start it. It’s a weird line to draw when the extra effort is 10 seconds (pop a pod in, press start),” stated one user on a Reddit forum for Airbnb hosts.
Other users pointed out that requiring guests to tidy up as a checkout requirement should not replace professional cleaning or home maintenance services between guests.
“Unless there is a dishwasher, guest should not be doing the dishes. Do you want to eat off dishes that a stranger washed in a hurry?” observed another Reddit user.

articles.title: Immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Most of the immigrants targeted by federal authorities in California this week for alleged voter fraud had applied for U.S. citizenship and now face charges related to lying on forms or during interviews. Those charges could lead to years in prison and thwart their efforts to naturalise.
Amandeep Kaur, who is among those charged, has lived in the country for eight years and is in the process of becoming a naturalised U.S. citizen, said her husband, Kulwinder Singh.

Mr. Singh said she got her driver's license in 2024 but took the written test at the DMV in Hindi because she struggles with English. He doesn't know if she registered to vote then. He said she received and returned a ballot in 2024 but they both thought it was a registration form.
Now, he said his wife is distraught with the news that she may have done something illegal.
“All she does is cry. It's heartbreaking,” said Mr. Singh, who is a U.S. citizen.

One of them is José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, who applied for citizenship in October 2025 after living in the country for 40 years and spending his entire adult life as a legal permanent resident. The federal government has alleged in charging documents that he improperly claimed to be a citizen in 2007 when registering to vote, then later lied about it on his immigration paperwork. The government hasn't accused him of casting a ballot.

Bañuelos-Díaz told The Associated Press he had no idea he had registered to vote until he was arrested on Monday (October 19, 2026) outside his Los Angeles home, though he recalls getting a driver's license around 2007. In California, people are prompted to register to vote when applying for a driver's license.
“I have never voted because I know I can't vote,” he said. “If there was a mistake, they should have called me out right away, not 20 years later.”
He was released from custody after his arrest but faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

Federal authorities on Monday (October 19, 2026) charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents in California in a crackdown on people accused of illegally voting or registering to do so. As of Thursday (October 22, 2026) morning, the government had filed charging documents in 10 of the 28 cases, offering additional details about how authorities relied on voter registration data to pursue broader criminal charges around immigration status.

Most of the immigrants charged in California have lived in the country for at least five years, and some of them for decades. They could face deportation if they lied on their citizenship application.
Immigrants convicted of illegally voting in the United States face up to a year in prison. Those convicted of lying on applications to become American citizens face up to a decade.

articles.title: The animals of ‘Dorothy’ and the hollow violence of male ego
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Dorothy , written and directed by Karthik Subbaraj, was released in theatres on September 25, and has taken viewers by storm . It is set in rural Madurai in the 1990s. It follows two young men, Subbu and Karthi, and the rigid ideas of masculinity and caste that test their friendship. When Dorothy arrives in their village, her presence challenges all their assumptions. Sananth, Rishikanth, and Keerthy Suresh play the principal roles, alongside Muthukumar as a powerful moneylender.

But as the humans of Dorothy impose their systems of domination and control on one another, try as they might, the natural world itself remains indifferent to the social hierarchies they consider so crucial.

In a recent interview, Mr. Subbaraj said he based the motif of the rooster in the film — which Subbu names and nurtures — on his research into Bahuchara Mata, a Hindu goddess associated with transgender communities and whose mount is a rooster. A festival centred on this deity is a guiding light in the film. Mr. Subbaraj also said the motif inspired the cockfighting scenes, and that he included it both to represent a piece of the Madurai landscape and to connote a higher meaning.

Many of the other animals of Dorothy are similarly part of the material world of rural Tamil Nadu and represent the human relationships unfolding within it. Some of the animals the people capture and slaughter or force them to fight or turn them into weapons against other people. On the other hand, the scorpion and the dung beetle act independently of human concerns, and in one serendipitous moment, set Karthi’s and Subbu’s shared journey on a very different path.

The skinned hare suspended from the ceiling in the house of Veeraiya, the local moneylender and Subbu’s father, paints an obvious picture of vulnerability stripped of protection, not coincidentally displayed in the home of a man who controls other people through economic dependence and caste power. There is also a disturbing parallel between the hare and Dorothy herself. The house is not just a place where people destroy vulnerable bodies but also normalise the cruelty of such actions.

Members of Veeraiya’s community also breed, train, and pit roosters and rams against one another for their entertainment. The visual meaning is obvious: it is the men that are really aggressive and territorial, seeking dominance over others. Their masculinity is animalistic. Yet all the cruelty we see on screen, especially all that matters to Dorothy , is entirely human, arising as it does from caste, property, honour, and gender expectations rather than anything nature imposes.

When the ram headbutts that poor man to death, an animal is become an instrument of human judgment. The violence is organised and conferred a social purpose, turning the scene into a commentary on the men, who have also conditioned themselves to fight and prove their masculinity. But then there are also the dung beetle and the scorpion, and the expansive verdant backdrop.

The animals in the film were computer-generated, and what the audience is asked to take away from their presence and actions in certain scenes is what the filmmakers have intended. That said, they themselves are not out of sorts with what we expect.

The landscape itself, from hilltop grasses to weeds in the dilapidated pond, from overgrown shrubs to forests in the distance, are real in both senses and just as important. As cinematographer Tirru said in an interview, the filmmakers deliberately placed people against these views to reveal the smallness of the men’s egos and the irrelevance of their prejudices within the world at large.

The scorpion is mindless of human authority and, by being itself, accidentally frustrates Karthi’s plan for a murder. When Karthi is treated for the sting, Subbu asks the doctor whether the poison has left his body — a question as much about the literal poison as the foul ideas filling his head and heart. The scorpion has thus become an agent of redemption.

The dung beetle, finally, made a curious, even amusing, appearance. It has nothing to do with the plot yet it cuts perhaps the most memorable figure. It appears rolling a dungball as three men brawl in the background. The choice reverses our usual hierarchy of attention, which is to put our selves and our needs first. But as the men risk their lives over their pernicious social expectations, rolling around in the figurative excrement they themselves have laid, the beetle simply gets on with its own, thoroughly unbothered.
Dung beetles also find their way using the moon and stars, being guided by the cosmos itself, whereas the people nearby have evidently lost their moral bearings.

articles.title: Butterfly migration: Blue tigers head towards Western Ghats with the onset of North-East monsoon
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: It is Ayudha Pooja day and Tiruchy Road in Coimbatore is at its busiest. Even as makeshift shops selling flowers and puffed rice do brisk business, in the skies above, something magical unfolds. We first spot them here and there: blue tiger and dark blue tiger butterflies, and a few common crows float above us. Soon, there are more. They seem to be everywhere. That is when we realise we are right on the migratory route of lakhs and lakhs of butterflies flying from the Eastern Ghats towards the Western Ghats to escape the North-East monsoon that is battering Chennai and its surrounding districts.

Butterfly watchers in cities along their path are on high alert. This is the moment they have been waiting for all year. Alerts on the WhatsApp group Butterfly Migration India invite men and women in places such as Salem, Erode, Tiruppur, Coimbatore, and Madurai, apart from Kerala, to step outside and count the butterflies.
Butterflies on their way to the Western Ghats | Photo Credit: DEEPAK KR

According to CV Nishanth, a core member of The Nature and Butterfly Society (TNBS) that was started as a Facebook group in 2013, some places in Coimbatore recorded as many as 100 to 120 individuals per minute. “There are blue and dark blue tigers, common and double banded crows, and a few emigrants,” he says. “In Kalapatty main road, 120 individuals were spotted per minute at 9.50am on October 18.” Nishanth says that they undertake this tedious journey to escape the rains and reach host plants in the forests of the Western Ghats.
Dark blue tiger butterflies observed during the ongoing migration from the hill ranges of the Eastern Ghats towards the Western Ghats | Photo Credit: SIVA SARAVANAN S

Dr Kalesh Sadasivan, a research associate with the Travancore Nature History Society and a member with the State Board for Wildlife, Kerala, says that once they make it to deep forest, they start a new chapter in life. “These butterflies start their journey after the pre-monsoon showers in the Eastern Ghats, flying past Tamil Nadu plains and the Mysore plateau,” he says. Once they reach their host plants, they feed, then mate. “After they lay eggs, they die,” he says.
Crow butterflies migrate from Eastern Ghats to the Western Ghats | Photo Credit: DEEPAK KR

To travel hundreds of kilometres only to perish? “Their subsequent generations — we don’t know which ones, perhaps the third or fourth — fly back to the Eastern Ghats around May when the pre-monsoon showers ahead of the South-West monsoon arrive,” he explains. The most fascinating aspect of this up and down journey, Dr Kalesh says, is the in-between months, when they wait for “environmental cues” at forest patches where there is plenty of food.

“Millions of them congregate on trees from January to February, simply waiting,” he says. They know it in their DNA when the time is right to fly back. Dr Kalesh, who has been part of several Forest Department surveys, has witnessed such large swathes of butterflies in the forests of Parambikulam. “They are fascinating to look at,” he recalls
A congregation of blue tigers and crows | Photo Credit: Ramanasaran Hari

A Pavendan, the founder and president of TNBS too has seen such massive butterfly congregations in Silent Valley in Kerala. “Entire trees will be covered inch to inch,” he says. As part of the TNBS, he has contributed to several Forest Department surveys and studies on butterflies and has been observing them since 2011. The migration, he says, takes place when skies are clear with very little cloud cover. “They don’t fly continuously,” he adds: “They settle down on trees by 3pm to rest, flying back the next morning.”

The sheer magnitude of the butterflies can take one’s breath away. Picture this: Pavendan says that when there is enough sunshine, around 100 individuals can be seen within a 50 to 100 metre distance. “So, 6,000 of them cross the same distance in an hour,” he says. While their flight pattern is scattered, if people looked up, they are sure to notice the delicate creatures, he adds.

articles.title: How is air pollution in Delhi-NCR ahead of winter?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The story so far: As the air quality of Delhi worsened to the ‘poor’ category in the national capital, the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and adjoining areas (CAQM) on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) announced Stage 1 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) in Delhi and the National Capital Regio n (NCR) to bring down the pollution.

Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November, and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

The GRAP or Graded Response Action Plan , is a set of short-term emergency measures to reduce air pollution and is divided into four stages. The CAQM announces the different stages, depending on the level of pollution recorded or forecast for the near future.

Whenever the CAQM announces GRAP, it directs State governments to implement the restrictions with “immediate effect” in entire Delhi and also in the NCR districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan. The restrictions will come into effect on the ground when respective State governments pass orders to implement them.
As per law, the State governments are bound to implement directions of the CAQM and the Commission can initiate legal action against officers not following its directions.

The GRAP was first notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in January, 2017, pursuant to Supreme Court directions to provide for graded measures corresponding to different levels of air quality.

Initially, the GRAP was implemented by the EPCA (Environmental Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority), which was formed in 1998 by the Supreme Court and was responsible for the management and coordination on air pollution in Delhi and the NCR.
But the EPCA was not backed by a statute and experts had raised the issue that it lacked the teeth to act against authorities which did not follow its orders.

In 2021, the CAQM replaced the EPCA and since then it has been implementing the GRAP. Over the years, at times after coming under attack of the Supreme Court, the GRAP has gone through multiple revisions, making it more stringent.
Most of the actions under Stage 1 are directing authorities to strictly implement existing norms related to air pollution.

The four stages of GRAP are: Stage I – ‘Poor’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI ranging between 201-300), Stage II – ‘Very Poor’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI ranging between 301-400), Stage III – ‘Severe’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI ranging between 401-450), Stage IV – ‘Severe +’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI > 450).
Though the GRAP can be imposed any time during the year, the higher stages of GRAP are mostly invoked during winter as air quality deteriorates.

articles.title: A greying population, a strained care system
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Girija (name changed) spent years working as a domestic worker before her failing knees made it difficult for her to continue. Hoping to find a more manageable way to earn a living, the 60-year-old borrowed money from acquaintances and set up a roadside vegetable stall. But another health problem emerged, making it difficult to keep the business running.

“She learnt that she was suffering from urinary incontinence. Taking frequent loo breaks while managing the stall was not practical, and she eventually decided to shut shop, losing her source of income in the process,” says Gurajada Sobha Pernidevi, founder-president of Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, a voluntary organisation working for the welfare of women.

For older people with limited financial means, a health problem can do more than cause physical discomfort; it can take away their livelihood, independence and opportunities to socialise. Conditions that are difficult to discuss, such as urinary incontinence, are often endured in silence because of embarrassment and the cost of managing them.

Unlike ailments that call for joint replacement surgery or a cardiac stent, these less visible difficulties of ageing often receive scant attention, despite their potential to disrupt daily life. However, as Telangana’s share of elderly population grows, addressing such overlooked needs will become increasingly important.

Telangana’s population aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 12.5% in 2026 to 17.1% in 2036, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s report, ‘State Finances — A Study of Budgets of 2025-26: Demographic Transition in India — Implications for State Finances’.

The State is expected to join the category of ageing ones, where senior citizens account for at least 15% of the population. The projected demographic shift raises questions about how healthcare, caregiving and community support can keep pace with the needs of older people, particularly those who live alone or cannot afford private services.
Associations working with senior citizens say the challenges range from obtaining medicines and reaching hospitals to finding dependable caregivers and accessing mental health support.

P. Shyam Kumar, State project coordinator at HelpAge India, says doorstep medical services, including palliative care, could make healthcare more accessible. Nutritional supplements and the delivery of medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists could also help older people manage their health.

“Without adequate support, their condition may deteriorate, leading to more hospital visits, additional expenses and greater dependence on family members. So, supplying medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists may work in this direction,” he adds.

Access to healthcare is not simply a matter of getting an appointment or obtaining medicines. Older people who depend on younger family members for hospital visits may have to wait until someone can take time off work and accompany them.

Members of several associations say a family member’s availability often influences whether and when an older person seeks medical attention. Those with limited mobility may need transport, a wheelchair or stretcher. In a multi-storey building without a suitable lift, even getting someone downstairs can require additional assistance and planning. Hospital visits can involve long walks between departments, diagnostic tests and consultations, making them particularly difficult for those without someone to accompany them.

The problem does not end at the hospital gate. For older people who cannot leave home, finding a doctor willing to make a home visit can be equally difficult. “This is a crucial requirement of those who are unable to step out of their house,” says Sobha.

articles.title: Shamonda virus, the livestock pathogen detected in human for the first time | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: France reported the first known human infection with Shamonda virus on October 22, 2026. The patient, who was severely immunocompromised and receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, died in early October. Investigations are underway to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the death, and how the patient acquired the infection.

French authorities suspect that the patient was infected by the bite of a Culicoides midge in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating among animals during spring and summer. The specific insect responsible has not been identified. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey.

French authorities say that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge of the virus. The World Health Organization (WHO) has also said that wider spread is unlikely based on the information currently available. However, investigations into the human case are continuing.

Shamonda virus is a vector-borne virus belonging to the genus Orthobunyavirus in the family Peribunyaviridae . It is part of the Simbu group of viruses, which also includes Schmallenberg virus and Akabane virus.

The virus was first isolated from cattle in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in parts of Africa and Japan. Before the recent case in France, it was considered an animal pathogen that did not infect humans.

Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although infections have also been detected in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. In livestock, infection can cause fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, loss of appetite and reduced milk production. In pregnant animals, it has been associated with abortions and congenital abnormalities in offspring.

Neurological signs have also been reported in horses infected with the virus in Europe. The extent to which the variants circulating in Europe differ in their effects on animal health remains under investigation.

The virus is understood to spread primarily through the bites of infected Culicoides midges, tiny blood-feeding insects. The precise midge species responsible for transmitting the European variants has not yet been established.

According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), there is currently no evidence of horizontal transmission, or spread between animals through direct contact or other routes. Vertical transmission, from a pregnant animal to its offspring, has been reported.

Two genetically distinct variants, designated Shamonda virus Europe 1 (SHAV-EU1) and Shamonda virus Europe 2 (SHAV-EU2), have been identified in Europe in 2026. Research indicates that they may have been introduced separately. Their geographical distribution, effects on livestock and long-term significance remain under investigation.

The detection in a human has raised questions about whether Shamonda virus can cause disease beyond its known animal hosts. French authorities have reported that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were considered very likely to be linked to the infection. However, investigations are continuing to establish whether the virus caused or contributed to the death.

The patient was severely immunocompromised and had an underlying serious illness. It is not yet known whether similar complications would occur in people with different health conditions or whether people without immune suppression could develop symptomatic infection.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.
